claims.statement: This page declares FPT/GHEC/GHES and administrator/edit-repository-rules permission. Branch/tag rules differ from push rules, whose availability is limited to eligible private/internal repositories and their forks; bypass can be granted to selected roles, teams or apps.
Across a fork network, root-repository push-ruleset bypass grants determine bypass in forks too.
Restrict creations permits only bypass actors to create matching branches/tags. Creation protection is distinct from update protection.
Restrict updates permits only bypass actors to push matching branches/tags; configured bypass must be evaluated separately.
Restrict deletions permits only bypass actors to delete matching branches/tags; the option is selected by default, not proof of its activation in a target.
Linear history disallows merge commits and therefore requires squash or rebase merging enabled; incompatible repository merge methods matter to applicability.

Merge-queue rules are gated to GHEC or GHES>=3.15 and can require merges through a queue at repository level; this rule is not available for organization-level rulesets. Optional settings below are source choices, not adopted defaults.

Queue configuration offers allowed merge method, build concurrency, minimum/maximum merge-group sizes and minimum-size wait time; concurrency limits requesting checks and merge_group.checks_requested dispatch, not group size. After wait time expires, a smaller group may merge.

Require all queue entries to pass checks can require each grouped entry’s checks, or only the group-head commit containing all grouped changes when disabled; this choice changes which revisions have passed validation.
Status-check timeout bounds waiting for any conclusion before treating checks without a conclusion as failed. It is a configurable value, not a universal local deadline.

Required deployments select successful deployment environments before merging; when repo-rules-enterprise applies, the included note says this rule is NOT available at organization level. Selecting environments is not proof of environment approval, recovery or rollback.

Required signatures demand verified signatures on pushed commits. For new branches rulesets check only commits unreachable from other branches, while classic protection checks only when matching-branch creation is restricted; branch updates check the entire specified commit range.
Signature references describe source verification behavior, not certification of a human author’s identity or adoption of mandatory signing.

The FPT/GHEC vigilant-mode reusable permits partially verified commits for users who enable vigilant mode. An unsigned commit can require signed rewriting and a force push; those exceptions affect compatible signing policy.

The signing reusable describes test-merge checking of introduced head commits: unsigned head commits can block even a GitHub-signed squash result, including for the PR author. Rewrite/sign or authorized bypass may be needed; GHES does not allow GitHub-side merging in this context. Signed local merges and any required-PR bypass need explicit review.
Require a pull request requires a PR before merging; by itself it does not require any approval.

Additional review settings govern approvals, stale reviews and code owners. Manual merging under stale-review or latest-push protection is rejected unless the generated merge content exactly matches GitHub’s result.

Required reviews allow changes through PRs approved by the required number of reviewers with write permission. A person requesting changes must subsequently approve; if that reviewer is unavailable a writer can dismiss the blocking review. Pending/rejected reviews on other PRs with the same head commit can also block merging.
Stale-approval dismissal responds to changed reviewed diff or merge base; this supports the pushed-diff predicate of RULE005 but the merge-base qualification remains additional source context.
For required code-owner review, any one of multiple owners for the affected code can satisfy the source requirement; the source does not require unanimous ownership approval.
Review dismissal permissions can be limited to chosen people, teams or apps through the UI, REST API or GraphQL; dismissal authority is distinct from obtaining required approvals.
Latest-reviewable-push approval must come from someone other than its pusher; this can preserve previous approvals while reducing the risk of an unreviewed final change.
Required conversation resolution blocks merging until all PR comments are resolved, meaning addressed or acknowledged; it is separate from approval count and code-owner review.
Allowed merge types must intersect with repository-enabled merge methods; disjoint choices block merging.

The FPT/GHEC public-preview extra-approval option is enabled by default for new and existing rulesets. It applies when Copilot OPENS a PR under its app identity without attribution to a person, requiring one more human write-access approval than configured; it does not describe Copilot approving a review.

The Copilot extra-approval option has no effect when configured approvals are zero. If cleared, only the configured count applies; a separately enabled latest-push requirement still needs approval covering the last push from someone other than Copilot.

Required team reviewers are gated to FPT/GHEC/GHES>=3.22: at most 15 teams; a team member’s approval counts only if that team has repository write permission or higher. Organization membership/scope must fit and user-owned repositories cannot use it.
A team may require 0–10 approvals; zero gives visibility without gating. File-pattern matching follows ordered gitignore semantics including negation, not the fnmatch semantics of branch targeting.

Required checks/statuses must pass before merging. Expected GitHub App selection requires the app installed with statuses:write, a recent check run and association with a pre-existing required check. Other publishers then block merging; any-source authors can still be manually inspected.
Optional do-not-require-checks-on-creation is gated to GHEC/GHES>=3.15 and permits branch creation regardless of check results; update requirements must not be inferred to cover creation.
For organization-level required statuses, only installed apps with statuses:write appear in configuration; this note is gated to repo-rules-enterprise.

Strict checks require an up-to-date branch; loose checks accept passed checks without updating to the target and may encounter integration failures; disabled checks allow merges irrespective of check results.

Block force pushes is selected by default and prevents users with push permission from force pushing, subject to bypass. Force pushing rewrites history and can discard collaborators’ commits; setting presence is not a rejection test.
Force-push blocking can also block administrator default-branch renaming absent bypass. Allowing force pushes does not override other protections such as linear history.

GHES site-level prohibition on all branches prevents repository force-push allowances; a default-branch-only site prohibition still permits allowing force pushes on other branches or tags. Evaluate the scope of this inherited constraint.

Secret-scanning merge protection is gated to FPT/GHEC/GHES>=3.24 and described as public preview; it scans the PR head and blocks while scanning is pending or qualifying introduced open alerts remain. It is not a certificate that all secrets or history were cleared.

The secret gate blocks a pending PR-head scan or a commit introducing an OPEN alert matching a selected secret TYPE. Provider, custom and generic patterns are supported; AI-detected secrets are not. Alert remediation and safe credential replacement remain separate work.

Required code-scanning results can select tools and severity thresholds. Missing setup, analyses still in progress or qualifying alerts can block merging; configured tools alone do not prove completed analysis for the relevant revision.

Code-quality protection is FPT/GHEC-only and blocks pending analysis, analysis failure (including exhausted Actions-minutes budget), or results at/above the configured severity. It does not specify a new-issue count budget.

Code-coverage protection is preview functionality requiring code quality enabled and coverage uploads. It checks aggregated PR-branch minimum line percentage and a maximum percentage-POINT drop relative to DEFAULT-branch coverage. It does not wait for uploads: require the upload-associated status checks to await all expected coverage evidence.

Required-workflow rules are gated to GHEC/GHES>=3.12, with enterprise scope additionally gated by enterprise-ruleset-workflow-rule (GHEC/GHES>=3.18). Source repository visibility constrains targets: public can target all, internal internal/private, private private; external reuse permissions matter.

Evaluate-mode passing workflow runs can be reused on activation, and PRs opened before Evaluate may merge without those runs. Observe the specific PR and enforcement state before claiming a required workflow ran.

The required workflow must specify one or more supported events in on:. Ruleset workflow events ignore branch, path and activity filters. Supported defaults are PR/PR-target opened, synchronize and reopened, and merge-group checks_requested; ordinary filter assumptions do not establish ruleset behavior.
Required-workflow rules block direct pushes and should target branches accepting PRs, not every branch. Optional creation-check bypass must be distinguished from update checks.

Enterprise metadata restrictions are gated to GHEC/GHES>3.10. The included metadata note says ALL commits on a squash-merged branch must satisfy the base branch metadata requirements, in conflict with this page’s later resulting-commit-only statement.

Metadata rules can constrain author/committer email, message or new branch/tag names with literal or regex patterns. Immutable metadata can require rebase/rewrite. Ref-update blocking still lets commits enter and be retrieved without being reachable from the rejected ref; other valid refs can update. GHES hooks are an alternative, not proven equivalent. Metadata consistency is not a content-security boundary.
To reduce contributor friction the source recommends restricting metadata on a limited branch set, with main plus PRs as an example; this is source advice, not local adoption.
For squash merges this page says individual PR commits are ignored and ONLY the resulting squash commit metadata is validated; this conflicts with the included all-commits requirement.
Committer-email patterns must include noreply@github.com to permit web merges and GitHub-created commits. Metadata rules apply to new commits from activation forward, not existing branch/tag history.
File-path push restrictions accept at most 200 entries of at most 200 characters using the included fnmatch examples. These pinned limits are not observed live quotas.
File-path allowed exceptions are gated to FPT/GHEC and use fnmatch, with validation when saving. An exception intentionally permits matching content; this does not automatically apply on GHES.
Path-length push restrictions block paths exceeding the configured limit, across the applicable push-ruleset fork scope.

Extension restrictions accept at most 200 entries of 200 characters. Allowed exceptions are only for path/size restrictions; a jar exception to a broad filename constraint should instead be expressed through path patterns.

File-size restrictions use a selected size limit; their FPT/GHEC allowed path exceptions may admit matching larger files. Restrictions and exceptions do not themselves satisfy the catalog’s approved artifact-storage objective.

scope: Primary reading of full pinned article and recursively included dependencies. Reviewed source statements only; no adoption or live platform verification.
